title: The Quartz Crisis

slides.title: The watch that almost killed *Swiss watchmaking.*
slides.body: A battery and a tiny crystal nearly wiped out centuries of tradition.

slides.title: A crystal that *vibrates*
slides.body: Run electricity through quartz and it vibrates at a remarkably steady rate: **32,768 times per second** in most quartz watches. Count the vibrations, and you have a near-perfect clock.

slides.title: The Swiss were *ahead*
slides.body: Swiss quartz prototypes dominate the 1967 Neuchâtel Observatory competition, **beating Seiko's entries.** Then Switzerland hesitates.

slides.title: Seiko *strikes*
slides.body: On Christmas Day, Seiko launches the Astron, **the world's first quartz wristwatch on sale.** Accurate to ±5 seconds a month. Price: 450,000 yen, about as much as a Toyota Corolla.

slides.title: …*slowly*
slides.body: The Swiss Beta 21 arrives in 1970, but the industry trusts its mechanical tradition. Meanwhile quartz gets **cheaper every year.**

slides.title: 1,600 watch firms become *600*
slides.body: Between 1970 and the mid-1980s, **about two in three Swiss watch jobs disappear**: from roughly 90,000 workers to around 30,000.

slides.title: The plastic *savior*
slides.body: The Swiss fight back with a cheap, colorful plastic watch made of just 51 parts. **Swatch sells over 2.5 million in two years.**

slides.title: Mechanical watches became *luxury*
slides.body: Quartz won the battle for accuracy. So Swiss mechanical watches stopped selling time and started selling **craft, history and emotion.**

slides.title: A crystal nearly ended it. *Plastic* saved it.

caption:
In 1969 a watch with a battery nearly ended centuries of Swiss watchmaking. ⚡

The twist: the Swiss had working quartz prototypes too, and they beat Seiko's in 1967. But Seiko put one on sale first. Within 15 years, two out of three Swiss watch jobs were gone, until a plastic watch called Swatch changed everything.
